nameStory: This honeysuckle gets its name from the Amur River region where China meets Russia, its native homeland in eastern Asia. Like other honeysuckles, it was named for the sweet nectar that can be drawn from its tubular flowers - a treat that children have enjoyed for generations by gently pulling the stamens through the flower tube.
description: Amur honeysuckle is a tall, upright shrub that can grow 10-15 feet high and equally wide, forming dense thickets over time. This non-native invader produces masses of small white flowers in late spring that age to yellow, followed by bright red berries that birds love to eat. Its oval leaves are arranged in pairs along the stems, and the shrub keeps its green foliage well into fall, often staying leafy after native plants have dropped their leaves. The bark on older stems is grayish-brown and develops a somewhat shreddy texture.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with a smooth, soft texture and no teeth along the edges. The leaves feel thin and papery when crushed and have a subtle sweet smell.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers about 3/4 inch long that start white and turn creamy yellow as they age, appearing in pairs along the branches in late spring. The flowers have a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's strongest in the evening.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about 1/4 inch across that appear in late summer, often in abundant clusters. The berries have a slightly bitter taste and contain several small seeds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a large, dense, multi-stemmed shrub with arching branches that create thick, impenetrable stands. Individual stems can be quite straight and upright when young.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature stems develop grayish-brown bark that peels in thin, papery strips. Young twigs are smooth and hollow between the leaf joints, making a satisfying snap when broken.

habitat: Thrives in forest edges, old fields, and disturbed woodland areas throughout New England, tolerating both sun and partial shade. It's particularly common along streams, in parks and suburban areas, and in the understory of deciduous and mixed forests. This adaptable invader can grow in various soil types and outcompetes native shrubs by leafing out early and holding its leaves late into fall.

seasonality.spring: Leafs out earlier than most native shrubs, giving it a competitive advantage. White tubular flowers appear in late spring, usually May, emerging in pairs along the branches with a sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade to yellow then drop, replaced by developing green berries. The full green foliage creates dense shade that suppresses native wildflowers and tree seedlings underneath.
seasonality.fall: Bright red berries ripen and become very noticeable against the still-green foliage. Unlike native shrubs, Amur honeysuckle keeps its leaves green well into fall, often into November.
seasonality.winter: Finally drops its leaves, revealing the multi-stemmed architecture and grayish, somewhat shreddy bark. Dried flower remnants and occasional persistent berries may still be visible on branches.

funFact: Amur honeysuckle is such an aggressive invader that it can completely transform a forest understory in just a few years, creating what ecologists call "green deserts" - areas so densely shaded by honeysuckle that virtually nothing else can grow underneath, eliminating the spring wildflowers that native forests are famous for.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with native elderberry, but elderberry has compound leaves (made up of several leaflets) while Amur honeysuckle has simple oval leaves. Remember: "Simple leaves, not so simple problem" - the simple leaves help identify this problematic invasive species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its sweet-sounding name and pretty flowers, Amur honeysuckle is considered one of the most destructive invasive shrubs in eastern North America. It was originally planted as an ornamental and for wildlife habitat, but its aggressive spread has made it a major target for removal efforts in many parks and nature preserves.
compareHints: Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches. It's much more aggressive than the native coral honeysuckle, which is actually a vine with trumpet-shaped red flowers. The key difference from other invasive honeysuckles like Tatarian honeysuckle is Amur honeysuckle's larger size and its habit of retaining green leaves well into fall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
